title: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: From 1501 to the 1860s about 12.5 million Africans were put aboard ships for the Americas; roughly 2 million died on the crossing. Ships under Portuguese and Brazilian, British, French, Spanish, Dutch, US and Danish flags carried them.
card: Between 1501 and 1867 slave ships embarked an estimated 12.5 million African men, women and children on the coasts of Africa and sold the survivors into bondage in the Americas. Portuguese and Brazilian vessels carried nearly half and British vessels about a quarter, with West Central Africa the largest source region. The traffic peaked in the late eighteenth century, and its last crossing arrived in Cuba in 1867.
what: The transatlantic slave trade was the forced shipment of Africans across the Atlantic to be enslaved in the Americas, carried out by merchants and ships of European and American states between the early sixteenth and the mid-nineteenth century. The SlaveVoyages database, built by David Eltis, David Richardson and collaborators from records of roughly 35,000 voyages (about 80 per cent of all that sailed), estimates that 12,521,337 people were embarked, in a series that begins in 1501. Vessels flying the Portuguese or Brazilian flag embarked about 5.85 million, British vessels 3.26 million, French 1.38 million, Spanish 1.06 million, Dutch 0.55 million, US 0.31 million and Danish or Baltic 0.11 million. Annual numbers were small in the sixteenth century, rose through the seventeenth, and reached about two million per quarter-century from the 1750s to the 1820s. West Central Africa supplied the largest share, around 5.7 million people, and the database documents embarkation regions from Senegambia to south-east Africa. Roughly 10.5 million people survived to be landed, over 90 per cent of them in the Caribbean, Central America and South America and fewer than half a million on the North American mainland. About 1.8 to 2.0 million died during the crossing or while waiting to sail, a figure derived here by subtraction rather than counted. Scholars have generally held that the Middle Passage grew somewhat less lethal over time, though the evidence is patchy and the Dutch data do not clearly show it. The trade shrank as states banned it, with British-flag voyages recorded in the database ending by the second quarter of the nineteenth century, but it continued under Spanish and Brazilian flags; the last slave ship to the United States landed in 1860 and the last transatlantic crossing reached Cuba in 1867. Estimates are revised as new voyages are found, so totals differ slightly between publications; the figures here come from the database tables and publications I could open.

uncertainty.note: 1501 is the first year of the database series (about 13,400 people are estimated for 1501-1525); earlier shipments of Africans to Iberia and Atlantic islands are outside the series. The estimates table runs to 1875 and the SlaveVoyages interface states coverage to 1866; 1867 is the date given for the last crossing to Cuba.

how: The trade ran as a chain of sales. Captives were taken in Africa by means this record does not document in detail, assembled at coastal embarkation points from Senegambia to south-east Africa, and sold to captains of ships fitted out in European and American ports, with West Central Africa the dominant source through most of the period. Ships then crossed on the Middle Passage, a voyage whose length depended on winds, currents and the distance between ports. Survivors were sold in Brazil, the Caribbean, Spanish America and North America, mostly to work on plantations, with sugar the leading driver. The volume rose from about 13,000 people in 1501-1525 to about 2 million in 1776-1800 as colonial plantation economies expanded and as Britain, France, the Dutch and others joined the Iberian carriers. National bans cut the trade by flag, but voyages continued under Spanish and Brazilian flags, to Cuba until 1867. Mortality fell somewhat over time according to most studies, though data are sparse.
why_it_matters: The trade moved more people across an ocean by force than any other migration of its era and shaped the demography of the Americas: over 90 per cent of the 10.5 million survivors were landed in the Caribbean, Central America and South America, and their descendants populate large parts of the hemisphere today. Its labour built the plantation economies of Brazil and the Caribbean, which in turn tied African coasts, European ports and American colonies into one commercial system; merchants, shipowners and states under seven flags profited from carrying people as cargo. Africa lost an estimated 12.5 million people to embarkation, with West Central Africa bearing the largest share, and about 2 million more died before landing. The memory of the trade continues to drive scholarship, memorialisation and debate over reparatory justice, a focus of UNESCO's Routes of Enslaved Peoples programme since 1994. Without the trade, the plantation colonies of the Americas could not have been worked at the scale or in the manner they were, the populations of Brazil and the Caribbean would have been radically different, and the African regions that lost the most people would have followed different demographic paths; how different is unknowable, but the direction is not in doubt. Its ending was gradual and uneven, and the persistence of slavery in Cuba until 1888 shows that ending the Atlantic traffic did not end enslavement.

related.because: European colonisation of the Americas that began after 1492 created the colonies and plantation economies to which captives were shipped from 1501 onward.

audience_note: This record describes the forced transport and enslavement of millions of people, including deaths in overcrowded ships. The media item is a period diagram showing how captives were packed aboard a ship; viewers may wish to be prepared before opening it.

importance.justification: One of the largest forced migrations in history, which shaped the populations, economies and political systems of Africa, the Americas and Europe for centuries.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the disembarked total (10.5 vs 10.7 million, hence the derived death range) and that I opened no source for Brazil's own disembarkation share or for national abolition-act dates.
